name.en: pork belly, cut into bite-size pieces
firm tofu, sliced into thick pieces

mistakes: Using fresh kimchi. Fresh kimchi makes a flat, sad stew. You want the sour, funky stuff that's been sitting in the fridge a while — the older, the better.
Skipping the stir-fry. If you dump everything into water at once, you get kimchi soup. Frying the kimchi in pork fat first is where all the depth comes from.
Forgetting the sesame oil at the end. One teaspoon drizzled on right before serving changes the whole aroma. Don't cook it — just finish with it.

steps.text: Heat a heavy pot over medium heat. Add the pork belly and kimchi and stir-fry until the kimchi softens and the pork loses its raw color, about 5 minutes. This step builds the base flavor, so don't rush it.
Pour in the water or broth. Stir in the gochugaru, soy sauce, sugar, garlic, and onion. Bring it to a rolling boil, then lower the heat to a steady simmer.
Lay the tofu slices gently on top. Spoon hot broth over them and simmer just until the tofu is heated through, so it doesn't break apart.
Taste and adjust: more soy sauce if it needs salt, a pinch of sugar if it's too sharp. Drizzle the sesame oil over the top, scatter the green onions, and serve it bubbling with a bowl of rice.

en.story: Kimchi jjigae was the first Korean dish I ever tried to cook, mostly because a YouTube thumbnail made it look foolproof. It was not. My first pot tasted like hot kimchi water. The fix turned out to be stupidly simple: the kimchi has to be properly sour, and the pork fat has to melt into the broth. Now it's the stew I make when I don't want to think.
en.title: Kimchi Jjigae
